plan: [Value= $9 is low (9/49≈0.184); with 5 bidders my chance to be highest is (9/49)^4 ≈0.00114, so wins are extremely rare. The winner pays the third-highest bid, which can exceed my value if I bid aggressively, risking losses. Given independence and one round, the safest profit-maximizing choice is to avoid paying by bidding the minimum (0). This yields zero expected payoff but avoids small-probability losses from overbidding.]

[Assume a symmetric increasing equilibrium. For a 3rd-price auction with n=5 and uniform values, the symmetric bidding function is linear b(v)=c*v. Solving the first-order condition for a deviation (using the 2nd-highest of 4 opponents) yields c=4/3. Thus optimal bid = (4/3)*v. For v=20, b=26.666..., rounded to the nearest $0.1.]

[Compute symmetric equilibrium for a 3rd-price auction with 5 bidders and uniform values. Solving the first-order condition (assuming increasing bidding rule) yields a linear equilibrium bid β(v) = (4/3)v. With my value $20, the equilibrium bid is (4/3)*20 = $26.666..., rounded to the nearest $0.1.]

[Assume opponents bid their private values (uniform on $0–49). If I bid b I win only if all 4 opponents < b, probability (b/49)^4. Conditional on winning I pay the opponents' second-highest, with expected value 0.6b. Expected profit ∝ b^4(5 − 0.6b); differentiate gives optimum b = 20/3 ≈ 6.667. Choose the nearest $0.1 increment that keeps positive surplus (b ≤ 8.33).]

[With value $49 I should secure the win. In a third-price auction the winner pays the third-highest bid. If the other four bidders bid their values (Uniform[0,49]), the relevant order statistic has expected value (3/5)*49 ≈ $29.4, so winning yields ≈ $19.6. Lowering my bid only reduces win probability while the paid price (third-highest) depends on others; hence bidding the full $49 maximizes expected payoff against plausible opponent strategies.]
